## Definition

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric parameter and data spaces, let $U\subseteq X$ be a nonempty admissible truth class, let $F:U\to Y$ be a forward map, and let $(Q,d_Q)$ be a metric target space. All metric spaces in this definition carry their Borel sigma-algebras. Give $U$ the subspace Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(U):=\{U\cap A:A\in\mathcal B(X)\}$, and assume that $q:U\to Q$ is measurable from $(U,\mathcal B(U))$ to $(Q,\mathcal B(Q))$. The target $q(x)$ is the recovery object assigned to truth $x$; $Q$ may be the parameter space itself or a quotient solution-class space. A **point reconstruction rule** is a Borel map $g:Y\to Q$, and its output at data $y$ is $g(y)$. A **learned point estimator** is such a map $\widehat q_\phi$ with a fitted parameter $\phi$ in a specified parameter set. A complete training description names the probability law $P_{\rm fit}$ of all variables used to fit $\phi$; those variables may be paired or unpaired. A complete test description names a probability law $P_{\rm test}$ for evaluation pairs $(Y,q(X))$. No equality between fitting and test laws is assumed.

A finite **unrolled learned update** consists of an integer $K\geq1$, a Borel initialization $u_0:Y\to Q$, and Borel maps $T_{\phi,k}:Q\times Y\to Q$ for $0\leq k<K$, with $u_{k+1}(y)=T_{\phi,k}(u_k(y),y)$. Its output $u_K(y)$ is a point reconstruction rule. An **amortized inverse map** is a learned point estimator applied to multiple data inputs after a single fit; this term adds a reuse convention, not an accuracy guarantee.

For a real Hilbert signal space $H$, a **denoiser** is a Borel map $D_\phi:H\to H$ trained under a specified signal-corruption law and used to transform a corrupted signal into a signal estimate or an update. A denoiser is the exact minimum mean-square error map only when it equals the conditional mean for the specified signal and corruption laws. A **learned prior** is a supplied Borel probability measure $\rho_\phi$ on $H$; one construction is the pushforward law $\rho_\phi(A)=\nu(G_\phi^{-1}(A))$ for $A\in\mathcal B(H)$, where $\nu$ is a specified probability measure on a measurable source space $(Z,\mathcal Z)$ and $G_\phi:(Z,\mathcal Z)\to(H,\mathcal B(H))$ is measurable. The law or generator alone is not a data-to-target estimator.

For a finite horizon $T>0$, a specified parameter set $\Phi$, and $\phi\in\Phi$, a **score field model** in a finite-dimensional signal space $\mathbb R^d$ is a Borel map $s_\phi:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ intended to approximate the target field $s^*(t,x)=\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$ for a specified family $(p_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ of positive continuously differentiable probability densities for which $s^*$ is jointly Borel. Its complete description names a probability law $P_{\rm fit}$ for all variables used to fit $\phi$ and a probability law $P_{\rm test}$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$ for evaluation inputs $(t,x)$; the target on those inputs is $s^*(t,x)$. These laws need not agree, and no approximation guarantee under either law is implied. A score field is not itself a posterior law, posterior sample, or point reconstruction rule. A **posterior sampler** is a probability kernel $S:Y\to Q$; relative to a supplied posterior target kernel $\Pi_y$, it is exact on a data domain $D$ when $S_y=\Pi_y$ as probability measures for every $y\in D$. A draw from $S_y$ is random; obtaining a point estimate from it requires an additional summary rule. The name “learned” by itself asserts no exact recovery, stability, convergence, calibration, or train-to-test guarantee.

## Example

In the InverseBench two-dimensional Navier–Stokes case, the spatial domain is the periodic square $(0,2\pi)^2$ (the flat torus). The velocity $u(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2$ is divergence-free, and its scalar vorticity is $w=\partial_1u_2-\partial_2u_1$. For viscosity $\nu>0$, forcing $f(x)$, and initial vorticity $w_0$, the forward model is

$$\partial_tw+u\cdot\nabla w=\nu\Delta w+f,\qquad \nabla\cdot u=0,\qquad w(\cdot,0)=w_0.$$

The reconstruction target is $z=w_0$; the observation is $y=PL(z)+n$, where $L$ is the numerical solution map from initial vorticity to vorticity at final time $T$, $P$ samples the final field, and $n$ is Gaussian measurement noise. InverseBench uses a pseudo-spectral solver with adaptive time stepping; the reported setup has a $128\times128$ grid, Reynolds number $200$, $10{,}000$ training samples, one validation sample, and ten test samples. The initial vorticity samples are drawn independently from the Gaussian random field $\mathcal N(0,(-\Delta+9I)^{-4})$, where $-\Delta$ is the negative Laplacian on the periodic square, and are evolved for five time units with the fixed forcing $f(x)=-4\cos(4x_2)$. The paper reports black-box forward access without a closed-form gradient for this implementation; the one-validation/ten-test split is part of this empirical benchmark, not a population-level guarantee.

## Example

In the InverseBench two-dimensional Navier–Stokes case, the spatial domain is the periodic square $(0,2\pi)^2$ (the flat torus). In the physical vorticity model, the periodic velocity $u(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2$ is divergence-free and its scalar curl is $\omega=\partial_1u_2-\partial_2u_1$. This curl has zero spatial mean. Taking the spatial mean of $u$ to be zero fixes the constant-velocity ambiguity. For viscosity $\nu>0$, forcing $f(x)=-4\cos(4x_2)$, and compatible initial curl $\omega_0$, the physical model is

$$\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega=\nu\Delta\omega+f,\qquad \nabla\cdot u=0,\qquad \omega(\cdot,0)=\omega_0.$$

The released benchmark uses a finite-grid scalar state denoted $w$. Its pinned solver computes velocity by Fourier streamfunction derivatives, which select zero spatial mean velocity and ignore the constant Fourier mode of the scalar state. The nonlinear term uses a dealiased state with zero mode removed, while the time-update formula retains the original state's zero mode; the specified forcing also has zero mean. Thus the solver defines a scalar-state extension even when $\overline w\ne0$. One must not identify such an entire state with the curl of a periodic velocity. In the corresponding continuum mean-split convention, $w=\overline w+\omega$, $-\Delta\psi=\omega$, and $u=(\partial_2\psi,-\partial_1\psi)$; only $\omega=w-\overline w$ is the curl, and $\overline w$ is a conserved scalar offset. This convention explains the zero-mode distinction; it does not assert that the finite-grid dealiased scheme is an exact continuum solution or that the released dataset has been projected to zero mean.

The reconstruction target is the supplied dataset field $z=w_0$ used as initial state for the inversion solver; the observation is $y=PL(z)+n$, where $L$ is this numerical scalar-state solution map over the specified inversion horizon $T$, $P$ samples the final field, and $n$ is Gaussian measurement noise. The dataset-generation horizon is a separate five time units: §4.1 and Appendix B.5 report independent Gaussian seed fields $\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,(-\Delta+9I)^{-4})$, evolved under the stated forcing for five time units to produce the dataset of nontrivial initial fields. Accordingly, $z$ denotes the evolved field, not a claim that the inversion-input distribution remains Gaussian with the seed covariance. On the full periodic space the reported covariance gives the constant eigenmode variance $9^{-4}>0$; the paper does not specify a zero-mode projection for the seed law. The scalar-state implementation permits retaining that offset without asserting the incompatible identity $w=\nabla\times u$ for arbitrary seeds.

InverseBench uses a pseudo-spectral solver with adaptive time stepping; the reported setup has a $128\times128$ grid, Reynolds number $200$, $10{,}000$ training samples, one validation sample, and ten test samples. The paper reports black-box forward access without a closed-form gradient for this implementation; the one-validation/ten-test split is part of this empirical benchmark, not a population-level guarantee.

In the InverseBench two-dimensional Navier–Stokes case, the spatial domain is the periodic square $(0,2\pi)^2$ (the flat torus). In the physical vorticity model, the periodic velocity $u(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2$ is divergence-free and its scalar curl is $\omega=\partial_1u_2-\partial_2u_1$. This curl has zero spatial mean. Taking the spatial mean of $u$ to be zero fixes the constant-velocity ambiguity. For viscosity $\nu>0$, forcing $f(x)=-4\cos(4x_2)$, and compatible initial curl $\omega_0$, the physical model is

$$\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega=\nu\Delta\omega+f,\qquad \nabla\cdot u=0,\qquad \omega(\cdot,0)=\omega_0.$$

The released benchmark uses a finite-grid scalar state denoted $w$. Its pinned solver computes velocity by Fourier streamfunction derivatives, which select zero spatial mean velocity and ignore the constant Fourier mode of the scalar state. The nonlinear term uses a dealiased state with zero mode removed, while the time-update formula retains the original state's zero mode; the specified forcing also has zero mean. Thus the solver defines a scalar-state extension even when $\overline w\ne0$. One must not identify such an entire state with the curl of a periodic velocity. In the corresponding continuum mean-split convention, $w=\overline w+\omega$, $-\Delta\psi=\omega$, and $u=(\partial_2\psi,-\partial_1\psi)$; only $\omega=w-\overline w$ is the curl, and $\overline w$ is a conserved scalar offset. This convention explains the zero-mode distinction; it does not assert that the finite-grid dealiased scheme is an exact continuum solution or that the released dataset has been projected to zero mean.

The reconstruction target is the supplied dataset field $z=w_0$ used as initial state for the inversion solver; the observation is $y=PL(z)+n$, where $L$ is this numerical scalar-state solution map over the specified inversion horizon $T$, $P$ samples the final field, and $n$ is Gaussian measurement noise. The dataset-generation horizon is a separate five time units: §4.1 and Appendix B.5 report independent Gaussian seed fields $\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,(-\Delta+9I)^{-4})$, evolved under the stated forcing for five time units to produce the dataset of nontrivial initial fields. Accordingly, $z$ denotes the evolved field, not a claim that the inversion-input distribution remains Gaussian with the seed covariance. On the full periodic space the reported covariance gives the constant eigenmode variance $9^{-4}>0$; the paper does not specify a zero-mode projection for the seed law. The scalar-state implementation permits retaining that offset without asserting the incompatible identity $w=\nabla\times u$ for arbitrary seeds.

InverseBench uses a pseudo-spectral solver with adaptive time stepping; the reported setup has a $128\times128$ grid, Reynolds number $200$, $10{,}000$ training samples, one validation sample, and ten test samples. The paper reports black-box forward access without a closed-form gradient for this implementation; the one-validation/ten-test split is part of this empirical benchmark, not a population-level guarantee.
